analysis.one_liner: Bans racial profiling by all law enforcement, lets victims sue, and ties federal police grants to anti-profiling policies.
analysis.headline: The End Racial Profiling Act of 2004 drew 127 cosponsors, including two Republicans, but never left a House Judiciary subcommittee and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal for any federal, state, local, or tribal law enforcement agent to use race, ethnicity, religion, or national origin in deciding whom to stop, search, or question. People harmed by profiling could sue for court orders to stop the practice, and statistics showing stops fall disproportionately on minorities would count as initial evidence. It would also require federal agencies to adopt anti-profiling policies and collect stop data, require states and cities to certify anti-profiling policies to keep major federal police grants, and fund training, complaint systems, and in-car cameras.
analysis.who_benefits: People subjected to traffic stops, pedestrian stops, frisks, searches, and workplace immigration checks based on race, ethnicity, religion, or national origin — disproportionately Black and Hispanic Americans and, after 9/11, Arab, Muslim, and South Asian communities. All of them would gain a federal right to sue and a legal prohibition backed by federal grant money. Communities that lose trust in police would benefit from mandatory data collection and complaint procedures, and the bill's findings cite Justice Department data showing searches of Black and Hispanic drivers were less likely to find contraband than searches of white drivers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People stopped or searched because of their race

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits every federal, state, local, and tribal law enforcement agent from relying on race, ethnicity, religion, or national origin in stops, searches, frisks, interviews, and workplace immigration checks [S2] [S3].

Lets individuals injured by profiling sue for court orders to end the practice, with statistical proof that a jurisdiction's stops fall disproportionately on minorities counting as prima facie evidence [S2] [S3].
Requires federal agencies to collect data on stops and searches, respond to complaints, and discipline agents who profile [S2] [S3].

Conditions the major federal police grant programs — Byrne, Cops on the Beat, and Local Law Enforcement Block Grants — on certification that a jurisdiction maintains anti-profiling policies, and funds training, data systems, and in-car cameras to detect profiling [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal, state, and local law enforcement agencies bear the cost: they would face a new legal prohibition, a private right of action, mandatory data collection and complaint systems, and the threat of losing federal grant funds if the Attorney General finds them out of compliance. Taxpayers fund the new grants and DOJ reporting. The bill's private right of action does not authorize money damages, limiting the direct cost of lawsuits.
analysis.who_pays_short: Law enforcement agencies and federal grant funds

drawbacks.text: The bill's own findings concede that the vast majority of law enforcement agents act without bias, and police groups argue a national prohibition imposes costly data-collection and reporting burdens on departments regardless of their actual conduct [S3].

Allowing disparate-impact statistics to serve as prima facie evidence means a department could face a federal lawsuit over stop patterns even where each individual stop was justified, a concern the bill text itself does not resolve [S3].

The grant conditions give the Attorney General power to withhold federal crime-fighting money from state and local governments, which opponents viewed as federal intrusion into local policing [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addressed a problem its own findings documented with Justice Department statistics: Black and Hispanic drivers who were searched were less likely to be carrying contraband than white drivers, meaning profiling was both discriminatory and ineffective as crime-fighting [S3]. The main costs fall on police departments, which would have to collect data and could lose grant money; the bill funds much of that compliance through grants and limits lawsuits to injunctive relief rather than damages. The serious design question is the disparate-impact trigger for lawsuits, which could sweep in departments whose individual stops were lawful.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in February 2004 and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, which sent it to its crime subcommittee in April; no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever followed, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: Rep. John Conyers introduced the bill on February 26, 2004, joined by over 100 original cosponsors including Nancy Pelosi and Richard Gephardt [S3] [S5].
It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced [S5].
On April 2, 2004, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security — the last recorded action of any kind [S5].
The bill ended the Congress with 127 cosponsors (124 Democrats, 1 Independent, 2 Republicans) but no committee vote and no floor vote in either chamber [S4] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Law enforcement agencies at every level came out ahead: no court-tested ban on profiling, no mandatory data collection, no complaint procedures, and no risk of losing Byrne, COPS, or block grant money. People subjected to profiling were left without the federal remedy the bill would have created.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Law enforcement agencies, untouched by the ban

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelmingly Democratic — 124 of 127 cosponsors — with only 2 Republicans signing on, and the Republican-run Judiciary Committee never scheduled the bill for action.

industries.industry: State, local, and tribal law enforcement agencies
industries.note: The bill would ban profiling practices, require data collection and complaint systems, and let grant money be withheld for noncompliance — but it also offers new federal grants for training, cameras, and data systems. Agencies gain money and lose unilateral discretion over stops and searches.
Best-practice grants could fund in-car video cameras, data-collection systems, early-warning software, and bias training, creating new public purchases.
The bill creates a new civil action for profiling victims and allows courts to award attorney's fees to prevailing plaintiffs.
